lesson.title: The X-Coordinate: Your Horizontal Address on the Plane
lesson.summary: The x-coordinate is the first number in an ordered pair, and it tells you exactly how far to move left or right from the origin.
lesson.body:
An ordered pair like (x, y) exists because a single number is not enough to describe a location on a flat surface. On a number line, one number pins down a point completely. But the coordinate plane has two directions to account for, horizontal and vertical, so it takes two numbers working together to locate a point. This need for two numbers rather than one is the entire reason the ordered pair exists as a tool in the first place. The x-coordinate is the first of those two numbers, and its whole job is to describe horizontal position: how far a point sits to the right or left of the vertical axis.

The sign of the x-coordinate carries real meaning, not just decoration. A positive x-coordinate means the point sits to the right of the origin, the fixed reference point where both axes meet. A negative x-coordinate means the point sits to the left. If the x-coordinate is exactly zero, the point cannot be left or right of center at all, so it must lie directly on the vertical axis. This mirrors how a plain number line works, except now that number line has been turned into just the horizontal half of a bigger picture. In fact, if you ignored the y-coordinate entirely and only looked at the x-axis, it would behave exactly like an ordinary number line, with the x-coordinate as the value being located on it.

Because the x-coordinate always comes first in an ordered pair, order is not optional. The pair (5, -2) and the pair (-2, 5) describe two completely different locations, even though they use the same two numbers. This is exactly why the pair is called "ordered": swapping the two values changes the point. A useful habit is to read (x, y) the same way every time, x first, and to say it out loud as "over x, then up or down y." This habit prevents a surprisingly common error where a student correctly finds both numbers but writes them in the wrong slots.

Here is a worked example that shows the x-coordinate doing real work. Suppose two points share the same y-coordinate, so they sit on the same horizontal line: point A is (2, 5) and point B is (x, 5). If B is known to be exactly 7 units to the right of A, what is the x-coordinate of B? Since moving right means adding to the x-coordinate, x = 2 + 7 = 9. Check the answer by measuring the horizontal distance between the two x-coordinates: |9 - 2| = 7, which matches the given distance exactly. So B is the point (9, 5). As a second check, notice that B should sit to the right of A, and since 9 is greater than 2, that direction checks out too.

The x-coordinate becomes even more useful once ordered pairs are plotted, since it is literally the instruction "move this many units left or right before doing anything else." It also connects directly to the y-coordinate, covered next: together the two numbers form a complete address, the same way a street number and a street name combine to locate a building, or the way a spreadsheet cell needs both a column letter and a row number. Neither number alone is enough, but paired correctly, they pin down one exact spot on the plane.
